svg.title: Video conferencing still stuttered after the circuit was doubled, because the bottleneck was jitter, upload capacity and queueing
svg.desc: Measured before the second upgrade: bandwidth was doubled from 100 to 200 Mbps yet the conference still stuttered. Round-trip time was acceptable at 45 ms, but jitter was 30 ms and loss around 0.6 percent, and the uplink was asymmetric at 300 down and 20 up. The three causes were real-time traffic sharing one queue with backup and file sync, the upstream direction saturating first, and no per-class queueing anywhere on the path. The fix was a dedicated priority queue, moving backup out of hours, and admission control on the uplink.
svg.text: The circuit was doubled and the video still stuttered
The upgrade added a resource that was not the constraint — the measurement that would have said so was never taken
WHAT WAS MEASURED
throughput on the circuit
100 → 200 Mbps after upgrade
round-trip time
45 ms — acceptable for RTP
jitter
30 ms — 6× the usable budget
packet loss
≈0.6% — visible artifacts
uplink, per direction
down 300 Mbps
up 20 Mbps — saturates first
what was never measured
jitter and loss per traffic class,
queue depth on the WAN edge,
bytes queued per participant
THREE CAUSES, NONE OF THEM BANDWIDTH
1 · one queue for everything
Real-time RTP competes with the nightly backup
and file sync in the same FIFO. Under a burst the
router drops whatever arrives — usually voice.
adding capacity just made the bursts bigger
2 · the wrong direction was sized
300 participants send video up as well as down;
20 Mbps of upstream cannot carry them, so the
encoder degrades and the queue builds upstream.
a symmetric-looking service was asymmetric
3 · no queue policy on the path
Even where QoS was configured, the marking was
stripped at a carrier hand-off, so the LLQ class was
always empty and best-effort carried everything.
a policy that does not survive the hand-off is decoration
THE FIX, IN ORDER OF EFFECT
1 · dedicated priority queue
LLQ/PQ for RTP, marked at the source end to end,
with the carrier contract requiring the marking to
survive every hand-off — verified per hop, not assumed.
2 · separate the bulk traffic
Backup and sync move to an off-peak window with a
hard rate limit, so they can never fill the queue
the conference depends on.
3 · size and police the upstream
Measure the up direction, cap it just below line rate,
and add admission control so participant 301 is
refused rather than degrading all 300.
4 · change the metric
Report jitter and loss per class, per minute. Throughput
was never the number that described the user's problem.
the dashboard now fails before the users do
Bandwidth answers "can it all fit". Voice and video ask "did it all arrive in the right order, in the right time".
Every upgrade must name the metric it intends to move. If the metric is not in the acceptance test, the upgrade cannot be shown to have worked.
The cheapest fix here was a queue, not a circuit — the circuit was bought because it was the only lever procurement knew how to pull.
